Trying to Conceive

How to Improve Sperm Quality: A Partner Health Checklist

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited by Mohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama — checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

To improve sperm quality, focus on the next two to three months: stop smoking and vaping, keep alcohol low, avoid hot tubs and saunas, work toward a healthy weight, and review medications, especially testosterone, with a clinician. Sperm take roughly two to three months to mature, so changes made today show up in the sperm present a season later. This checklist walks you through each step and when to start.

Start about three months before you want to try

Sperm are not stored up from years past. The body makes them continuously, and a single sperm cell takes roughly two to three months to develop from start to finish. That lag is the most useful fact in this whole checklist. The sperm present at a conception attempt in November began forming in August. So the habits you change today do not help this week; they help a season from now. This is good news, not bad. It means the window for meaningful improvement is short and concrete, and it means past habits do not lock in a permanent result.

If you can, start the checklist about three months before you begin trying. Month one: quit smoking and vaping, set a realistic alcohol limit, and book a routine checkup to review medications and any chronic conditions. Month two: keep going, skip hot tubs and saunas, and settle into regular meals and movement. Month three: hold the routine steady while the newest, healthiest sperm mature. If you are already trying, do not treat the timeline as a reason to pause. Start the same steps now; the improvements simply arrive on a rolling basis over the following months.

Quit smoking and vaping, and rethink alcohol

Smoking is consistently linked to lower sperm count, weaker movement, and more DNA damage inside sperm. Vaping is not a proven safe swap; nicotine itself appears to affect sperm, and vape products carry their own unknowns. Quitting is the single highest-value item on this list, and it also protects the household later, since secondhand smoke matters for pregnancy and for babies. Quitting is hard, so use real support: nicotine replacement, prescription options discussed with a clinician, a quit line, or an app. Set a quit date near the start of your three-month window so the recovery time overlaps with new sperm development.

Heavy or regular drinking can lower testosterone, reduce sperm production, and affect sperm shape and movement. The evidence on light drinking is less clear, so most guidance lands on moderation rather than fear: keep intake low and avoid binge drinking while trying. If cutting back is a struggle, that is worth an honest conversation with a clinician, not a private battle. Cannabis and other recreational drugs are also linked to poorer sperm quality, so the trying window is a sensible time to stop. What your partner drinks matters for their own preconception health too, but that is a separate conversation with its own guidance.

Keep the heat down

Sperm develop best a little below core body temperature, which is why the testes sit outside the body. Regular time in hot tubs, saunas, or very hot baths raises that temperature for long stretches and has been associated with reduced sperm quality. A fever can do the same thing for several weeks afterward. The practical move while trying is simple: skip hot soaks and sauna sessions, and keep showers at a normal temperature. This is a precaution, not a punishment. One accidental soak will not undo months of effort, and for most people the effect of heat appears to fade once the exposure stops.

Everyday heat sources are worth a lighter touch. A laptop resting directly on the lap for hours, heated car seats on long commutes, and long stretches of cycling in tight gear can all add warmth, though the evidence for these is weaker than for hot tubs. You do not need to redesign your life; move the laptop to a desk or a cushion and take breaks on long rides. Underwear choice gets a lot of attention online, and looser styles may help a little, but it is a small lever compared with smoking, alcohol, heat soaks, and medications. Spend your energy on the big items first.

Review medications, especially testosterone

Some common medicines can affect sperm production, and the biggest offender surprises many people: testosterone. Testosterone therapy and anabolic steroids tell the brain that the body has plenty of testosterone, so it stops sending the signals that drive sperm production inside the testes. Sperm counts can fall very low, sometimes to zero, and recovery after stopping can take months or longer. Testosterone is not a fertility booster; it works in the opposite direction. If you use prescribed testosterone, or you have used steroids for training, tell a clinician that you are planning for a baby. There are supervised ways to manage the transition, and stopping suddenly on your own is not one of them.

Other medicines deserve a look too. Some treatments for hair loss, blood pressure, depression, pain, and autoimmune conditions can influence sperm, and so can past chemotherapy. Do not stop anything on your own; untreated conditions carry their own risks. Instead, bring a full list, including supplements and over-the-counter products, to a routine visit and ask whether anything is worth adjusting before trying. The same visit is a good time to manage chronic conditions such as diabetes, and to ask about anything in your history, such as an undescended testis, mumps after childhood, or a known varicocele. If nothing is found, you leave with reassurance. If something is found, you found it three months early. One thing should not wait for the timeline: a new lump, swelling, or ache in a testicle needs a prompt appointment of its own, and sudden severe testicular pain is an emergency.

Weight, food, sleep, and keeping it sustainable

Carrying extra weight is associated with lower sperm quality and hormone changes, and working toward a healthier weight can help. Aim for gradual change through regular meals and movement you can actually repeat, not a crash diet, which is its own stress on the body. On food, the boring advice is the good advice: plenty of vegetables and fruit, whole grains, fish, nuts, and less ultra-processed food. A basic pattern like that covers most of what sperm need, including antioxidants and healthy fats. Supplements marketed for male fertility are heavily promoted and lightly proven; ask a clinician before spending on them.

Sleep and stress belong on the list too, mostly because they hold everything else together. Chronic short sleep and constant stress make it harder to quit smoking, drink less, and eat regularly, and both are linked with hormone disruption. Pick changes you can sustain for three months, not a perfect week that collapses. It helps to write the plan down: a quit date, an alcohol limit, the checkup booked, hot tubs paused. Some couples keep these notes and questions in the BeMama app alongside cycle dates, so nothing gets lost before an appointment. And if you have been trying for a while without success, ask about a fertility evaluation; there is separate guidance on when that makes sense.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Fertility is influenced by many factors, and no food, supplement, timing trick, or lifestyle routine guarantees conception. A varied eating pattern, appropriate activity, avoiding smoking and drugs, and reviewing alcohol, medicines, and workplace exposures support general preconception health for both partners.

Male fertility can also be affected by age, smoking, heavy alcohol or drug use, certain medicines and treatments, heat exposure, and health conditions. Persistent concerns deserve medical assessment rather than increasingly restrictive diets or unproven supplements.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to note meals, habits, supplements, and questions you want to discuss. The app does not score fertility, semen quality, or whether a particular diet increases the chance of pregnancy.

When to seek help

Check supplements and major diet changes with a healthcare professional, especially when you take medicine or have a medical condition.

Sources and further reading

  • CDC — Infertility: Frequently Asked Questions

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Sperm take roughly two to three months to mature, so start changes about three months before trying.
  • Quitting smoking and vaping is the highest-value step, and vaping is not a proven safe swap.
  • Skip hot tubs and saunas while trying; regular heat exposure is linked to lower sperm quality.
  • Testosterone therapy and anabolic steroids suppress sperm production, so review them with a clinician instead of stopping suddenly.
  • Steady food, movement, sleep, and managed health conditions support sperm more than any supplement.

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to improve sperm quality?

Roughly two to three months, because that is how long a sperm cell takes to develop from start to finish. Changes you make today show up in the sperm present about a season later. That is why most preconception advice for partners suggests starting around three months before you begin trying. Improvement is gradual, not instant.

Does smoking affect sperm?

Yes. Smoking is linked to lower sperm count, poorer movement, and more DNA damage in sperm, and vaping has not been shown to be a safe alternative. Quitting is one of the most useful things a partner can do before trying, and the benefits build over the following months as new sperm mature.

Do hot tubs affect sperm?

They can. Sperm develop best a little below core body temperature, and regular soaking in hot tubs, saunas, or very hot baths has been associated with reduced sperm quality. The effect appears reversible for many people once the heat stops, though recovery can take a few months. Skipping hot soaks while trying is a simple precaution.

Does testosterone lower sperm count?

Yes. Testosterone therapy and anabolic steroids can suppress sperm production, sometimes down to zero, because outside testosterone signals the body to stop driving sperm production in the testes. That is why testosterone is not a fertility treatment. If you use testosterone or steroids and want to conceive, ask a clinician about a supervised plan rather than stopping suddenly.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
